does vxworks has mkfifo

AI Mode reply for does vxworks has mkfifo

No, VxWorks does not natively support the POSIX mkfifo() function or standard Linux-style FIFO files. 
While VxWorks does support named pipes, its architecture, APIs, and underlying behavior differ significantly from traditional UNIX/Linux operating systems. 
How VxWorks Handles Named Pipes
Instead of mkfifo(), VxWorks uses its own proprietary pipeDrv (Pipe Driver) subsystem. To create a named pipe in VxWorks, you use the following function: 
c
STATUS pipeDevCreate (char *name, int nMessages, int cbMessage);
Use code with caution.
Key Differences Between VxWorks and Linux Pipes
FeatureVxWorks Pipes (pipeDevCreate)Linux/POSIX Pipes (mkfifo)
Creation APIpipeDevCreate("/pipe/my_pipe", max_msgs, msg_len)mkfifo("/path/to/fifo", mode)
Underlying EngineBuilt on top of VxWorks Message Queues (msgQ).Implemented natively via the virtual file system (VFS).
Data NatureMessage-oriented. It preserves packet boundaries.Stream-oriented. It processes data byte-by-byte.
Buffer OverflowIf a reader's buffer is smaller than the incoming message, the extra data is discarded.The reader simply blocks or reads up to the requested byte capacity without losing data.
File System PresenceNamed using an I/O device path format, but they do not exist as static files on physical storage.Created as actual special FIFO file nodes within the file system layout.
If you are porting code from Linux to VxWorks, you will need to replace your mkfifo() logic with pipeDevCreate(), and ensure that your read() and write() calls accommodate fixed message sizes rather than continuous streams. 
If you are modifying a specific codebase, let me know: 
  • Are you porting an existing POSIX/Linux application to VxWorks?
  • Do your pipes require stream-based communication or can they work with fixed-size messages?
  • Which VxWorks version (e.g., VxWorks 7) are you targets deploying to? 
I can provide a tailored code snippet to map your Linux IPC structure to VxWorks.

is there a way to generate a file for a software to block reading from it under vxworks?

AI Mode reply for is there a way to generate a file for a software to block reading from it under vxworks?

No, you cannot generate a standard static file on a regular file system (like dosFs or HRFS) that will cause a read() call to block indefinitely. 
In VxWorks, standard files always behave as stream abstractions that have an end. When a software application calls read() on a standard file, the file system driver (dosFsLib / hrfsLib) immediately calculates the current file pointer offset against the total file size. If the software reaches the end of the file, read() does not block—it immediately returns 0 (EOF). 
If your goal is to force a software application to block on a read() call until another process or the kernel feeds it data, you must use a virtual device file. 
The Recommended Solutions
1. The Virtual Device Path: pipeDrv (Named Pipe) 
The cleanest way to mimic a "blocking file" in VxWorks is to register a virtual named device path via the pipe driver (pipeDrv). The target software can still use standard open() and read() calls, but the driver will force it to block when no data is available. 
You can dynamically instantiate this pipe directly from your startup script, a Kernel Shell, or a Downloadable Kernel Module (DKM). 
How to create it in the VxWorks Shell / Script: 
c
/* Creates a virtual device file path /pipe/my_block_file */
/* Parameters: Device name, max unread messages, max message size */
pipeDevCreate ("/pipe/my_block_file", 20, 256);
Use code with caution.
Target Software Behavior: 
c
int fd = open("/pipe/my_block_file", O_RDONLY, 0);

// This call will BLOCKED indefinitely until another task 
// performs a write() to "/pipe/my_block_file"
int bytesRead = read(fd, buffer, sizeof(buffer));
Use code with caution.
Note on VxWorks pipes: Unlike Linux pipes which are byte streams, VxWorks pipes are built on message queues (msgQ). Ensure the software reading from it passes a buffer large enough to hold the maximum message size configured in pipeDevCreate, otherwise overflow data is discarded. 
2. The Custom Pseudodevice Driver 
If the target software strictly expects a custom device protocol or you need it to block unconditionally on a custom path (e.g. /dev/blocking_node), you can write a tiny kernel pseudo-driver utilizing iosDrvInstall(). 
You can implement the read function pointer within your driver structure to explicitly block the calling task by pending on a binary semaphore: 
c
#include <vxWorks.h>
#include <ioLib.h>
#include <semLib.h>

SEM_ID blockSem;
int myDrvNum;

/* Custom blocking read routine */
STATUS myCustomRead (int dummy, char *buffer, int maxBytes)
{
    // This forces the calling software thread to block/pend until semGive is called
    semTake(blockSem, WAIT_FOREVER);
    
    // Simulate or copy actual data here if unblocked
    buffer[0] = 'A';
    return 1; 
}

void installBlockingDevice(void)
{
    blockSem = semBCreate(SEM_Q_FIFO, SEM_EMPTY);
    
    // Install driver with null functions except for read
    myDrvNum = iosDrvInstall(NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, myCustomRead, NULL, NULL);
    
    // Create the "file" node
    iosDevAdd(malloc(sizeof(DEV_HDR)), "/dev/blocking_node", myDrvNum);
}
Use code with caution.
Summary Comparison
Implementation StrategyWill standard read() block?Code modification required?
Standard File on SD Card/Disk❌ No. Immediately returns 0 (EOF) at end-of-file.None.
pipeDevCreate() Virtual NodeYes. Blocks until a data packet is pushed.Change target path string to /pipe/...
Custom iosDrvInstall() DriverYes. Full control over exact blocking rules.Requires executing DKM setup code.
To refine this approach for your deployment, let me know:
  • Is the target software running inside a Real-Time Process (RTP) or in Kernel Space?
  • Can you easily modify the file path string inside the target software to point to a /pipe/ prefix?
  • Are you trying to simulate hardware behavior, or build a one-way inter-task communication (IPC) loop?

The target software is RTP, file path string can be different string without prefix, and I am simulate HW behavior for interrupt to test a interrupt listener software developed on block read a file provided by final driver (not available during development)

AI Mode reply for The target software is RTP, file path string can be different string without prefix, and I am simulate HW behavior for interrupt to test a interrupt listener software developed on block read a file provided by final driver (not available during development)

Since your target software runs inside a Real-Time Process (RTP), you face architectural constraints imposed by the Memory Management Unit (MMU): RTPs operate in user-space and cannot directly invoke kernel drivers (iosDrvInstall) or directly handle hardware Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). 
To accurately simulate an interrupt-driven hardware driver path without modifying your RTP listener code or utilizing the missing driver, your best strategy is to map a Public Named Pipe. In VxWorks, a named pipe acts as an I/O device path visible to the RTP, but you can feed it from kernel space (simulating the hardware interrupt). 
The Interrupt Simulation Architecture
Instead of dealing with file system files, you will trick the RTP by pointing its target file path configuration directly to a custom virtual device string (e.g., /your_custom_hw_path). 
 [ Kernel Space / ISR Simulator ]  --> writes to --> [ Named Pipe Device ] 
                                                             |
                                                       (Blocks Read)
                                                             v
                                                   [ RTP Interrupt Listener ]
Step 1: Create the Virtual Device from Kernel Space
Because the actual device path initialization belongs to the driver infrastructure, you must create the simulation node from the VxWorks Kernel context (via a startup script, DKM, or Kernel Shell). 
Use pipeDevCreate() to spin up a public, named object. You can name it anything to match your eventual driver's target filename scheme. 
c
/* Run this logic in Kernel space (e.g., via DKM or Kernel Shell) */
#include <pipeDrv.h>

void setup_hw_simulation(void) 
{
    /* 
     * Creates a blocking path named exactly what your software expects.
     * Arguments: Path name, Max Backlog Interrupts, Bytes per Event packet
     */
    pipeDevCreate("/your_custom_hw_path", 10, sizeof(uint32_t));
}
Use code with caution.
Step 2: The RTP Interrupt Listener Code
Your RTP application opens this path exactly as if it were a local physical device file. The read() function will block natively until a "simulation interrupt" triggers a data push. 
c
/* Run this logic inside your User-Space RTP Application (.vxe) */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdint.h>

void interrupt_listener_task(void)
{
    // The path can match the eventual final hardware driver target node
    int fd = open("/your_custom_hw_path", O_RDONLY, 0);
    if (fd < 0) {
        printf("Failed to connect to simulated device\n");
        return;
    }

    uint32_t interrupt_status = 0;
    printf("Listener active. Waiting for hardware interrupts...\n");

    while (1) {
        /* 
         * This read call BLOCKS automatically. 
         * It will unpend the moment the simulator pushes an event.
         */
        ssize_t bytesReceived = read(fd, &interrupt_status, sizeof(interrupt_status));
        
        if (bytesReceived > 0) {
            // Process your simulated interrupt vector safely inside user-space
            printf("[RTP Alert] Simulated Hardware Interrupt Received! Vector: 0x%08X\n", 
                   interrupt_status);
        }
    }
    close(fd);
}
Use code with caution.
Step 3: Triggering the "Interrupts" for Testing
To simulate the hardware line changing state or firing an ISR, you can run a quick trigger task inside Kernel Space (or link it to a hardware timer watchdog). 
Note: The VxWorks pipe driver is one of the few core elements explicitly designed to allow direct writing from a true hardware ISR context without crashing the system. 
c
/* Run this from Kernel space to fire your mock interrupts */
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdint.h>

void trigger_mock_interrupt(uint32_t mock_vector)
{
    int fd = open("/your_custom_hw_path", O_WRONLY, 0);
    if (fd >= 0) {
        // Writing to the pipe unblocks the RTP's read() statement instantly
        write(fd, &mock_vector, sizeof(mock_vector));
        close(fd);
    }
}
Use code with caution.
Key Considerations for Testing
  1. Packet Boundary Semantics: VxWorks pipes are message-queue based rather than a standard Linux continuous stream. Ensure that the size of the buffer you pass to read() inside your RTP matches or exceeds the nBytes block size configured inside pipeDevCreate(). 
  2. Clean Up: If you need to reset your simulation environment on the fly without rebooting the target hardware, you can tear down the simulation node from the Kernel Shell using pipeDevDelete("/your_custom_hw_path", TRUE). 
Would you like assistance writing a host-side test script or a Kernel Watchdog Timer routine to cycle these mock hardware interrupts automatically during your testing phases?

does vxworks support message queue?

AI Mode reply for does vxworks support message queue?

Yes, VxWorks natively supports message queues, and they are the primary, most efficient mechanism for inter-task communication (IPC) and synchronization within the operating system. 
VxWorks provides two distinct flavors of message queues: Native VxWorks Message Queues (msgQLib) and POSIX Message Queues (mqPxLib). Because your target application is running as a user-space Real-Time Process (RTP), you can safely use both types to communicate between RTP tasks or across the Kernel/RTP boundary. 
The Two Types of Message Queues in VxWorks
FeatureNative VxWorks Queues (msgQLib) [1]POSIX Message Queues (mqPxLib)
API Header#include <msgQLib.h> [1]#include <mqPxLib.h> (or <mqueue.h>)
Primary FunctionsmsgQCreate(), msgQSend(), msgQReceive() [1]mq_open(), mq_send(), mq_receive()
Scope OptionsPrivate (same RTP/Kernel) or Public (cross-boundary via msgQOpen)Always accessible system-wide via a pseudo-filesystem path (e.g., /mq0).
Task UrgencySupports high-priority message insertion (MSG_PRI_URGENT) at the front of the queue [1].Supports structural numerical message priorities (0 to 31).
Timeout SpecsSpecified in system clock ticks (or WAIT_FOREVER / NO_WAIT) [1].Specified via a POSIX real-time timespec absolute time structure.
Native VxWorks Message Queue Example (For RTP)
Because you are working with an RTP, you can create a Public Message Queue [1]. This allows a Kernel-space simulation module (like your mock hardware interrupt driver) to push data directly into a user-space RTP listener task. 
1. The RTP Listener Task (User-Space) 
The RTP application creates a public queue using a string descriptor so that external processes can bind to it. 
c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <msgQLib.h> /* Native VxWorks Message Queue Library */ [1]

#define MAX_MSGS 10
#define MSG_SIZE sizeof(uint32_t)

void rtp_msg_listener(void) 
{
    /* Create a PUBLIC message queue visible across the whole system */
    MSG_Q_ID myMsgQ = msgQCreate("/my_interrupt_q", MAX_MSGS, MSG_SIZE, 
                                 MSG_Q_FIFO, OM_CREATE | OM_EXCL); [1]
    
    if (myMsgQ == MSG_Q_ID_NULL) {
        printf("Failed to create message queue\n");
        return;
    }

    uint32_t received_vector;
    printf("RTP Listener waiting for message-queue interrupt events...\n");

    while (1) {
        /* This blocks natively until a message arrives */
        ssize_t bytes = msgQReceive(myMsgQ, (char *)&received_vector, 
                                    MSG_SIZE, WAIT_FOREVER); [1]
        
        if (bytes != ERROR) {
            printf("[RTP] Handled message queue event vector: 0x%08X\n", received_vector);
        }
    }
}
Use code with caution.
2. The Kernel Trigger Context (Simulating Hardware) 
Your kernel-side testing code or mock ISR locates the public queue by name and injects data directly into it. 
c
#include <vxWorks.h>
#include <msgQLib.h> [1]

void trigger_mock_hardware_event(uint32_t vector) 
{
    /* Bind to the existing public queue created by the RTP */
    MSG_Q_ID rtpQueue = msgQOpen("/my_interrupt_q", 0, 0, 0, 0, 0);
    
    if (rtpQueue != MSG_Q_ID_NULL) {
        /* Send data. Can use MSG_PRI_URGENT to jump to the front of the line */
        msgQSend(rtpQueue, (char *)&vector, sizeof(vector), 
                 WAIT_FOREVER, MSG_PRI_NORMAL); [1]
        
        msgQClose(rtpQueue);
    }
}
Use code with caution.
Why pick Message Queues over Named Pipes (pipeDrv)?
Since your final product will rely on a custom hardware file driver (using a standard read() operation), sticking to Named Pipes (pipeDrv) remains the superior choice for your current simulation phase because it lets you test your exact user-space I/O logic (open/read/close) without rewriting the application's underlying code framework. 
However, if you are looking to build raw, high-performance Inter-Process Communication (IPC) layouts between two software components later on, native msgQLib provides lower overhead than the file-system I/O layer [1]. 
Would you like to try a conceptual check to see how well you understand VxWorks inter-task communication? I can spin up a quick interactive quiz covering queues, pipes, and tasks.

      I am looking for a solution that can run the test on both linux and vxworks.

      AI Mode reply for I am looking for a solution that can run the test on both linux and vxworks.

      To achieve a single solution that compiles and runs seamlessly on both Linux and VxWorks (RTP) without changing your core framework code, you should use POSIX Message Queues (mqueue.h). 
      Both Linux and VxWorks natively support POSIX message queues. This allows you to simulate your hardware driver's behavior across environments without relying on OS-specific code wrapper hacks. 
      Cross-Platform Architecture
       [ Cross-Platform Test Trigger / Mock ISR ] --> mq_send() --> [ POSIX Message Queue ] 
                                                                       |
                                                                  (Blocks Read)
                                                                       v
                                                             [ Your RTP / Linux App ]
      1. The Cross-Platform Listener Code (Your Software)
      This module compiles identically on Linux and VxWorks. It uses standard POSIX syntax to block-read the queue, awaiting simulated "hardware events." 
      c
      #include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <mqueue.h>  /* Standard POSIX Message Queue Header */
#include <stdint.h>

#define QUEUE_NAME "/hw_interrupt_q"
#define MSG_SIZE   sizeof(uint32_t)

void run_interrupt_listener(void) 
{
    mqd_t mq;
    struct mq_attr attr;
    uint32_t interrupt_vector;

    // Define queue structure
    attr.mq_flags = 0;       // Blocking mode
    attr.mq_maxmsg = 10;     // Max messages in backlog
    attr.mq_msgsize = MSG_SIZE; 
    attr.mq_curmsgs = 0;

    // Open/Create the POSIX queue
    mq = mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_CREAT | O_RDONLY, 0666, &attr);
    if (mq == (mqd_t)-1) {
        perror("mq_open failed");
        return;
    }

    printf("Listener started. Blocking until hardware interrupt event arrives...\n");

    while (1) {
        /* 
         * This call BLOCKS natively on both Linux and VxWorks 
         * until data is pushed into the queue.
         */
        ssize_t bytes_read = mq_receive(mq, (char *)&interrupt_vector, MSG_SIZE, NULL);
        
        if (bytes_read >= 0) {
            printf("[SW Target] Caught simulated interrupt vector: 0x%08X\n", interrupt_vector);
        } else {
            perror("mq_receive error");
        }
    }

    mq_close(mq);
}
      Use code with caution.
      2. The Cross-Platform Test Framework (The Injector)
      To simulate the hardware interrupt firing during your automated testing sequences, this snippet writes the event into the named queue. It runs seamlessly inside a Linux simulation test bench or a VxWorks Kernel/RTP shell execution context. 
      c
      #include <stdio.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <mqueue.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#define QUEUE_NAME "/hw_interrupt_q"

void simulate_hw_interrupt_fire(uint32_t mock_vector) 
{
    // Open the queue in write-only mode
    mqd_t mq = mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_WRONLY);
    
    if (mq != (mqd_t)-1) {
        printf("[Test Framework] Triggering mock interrupt line (Vector 0x%08X)\n", mock_vector);
        
        // Inject data. The listener's mq_receive breaks its block immediately.
        mq_send(mq, (const char *)&mock_vector, sizeof(mock_vector), 0);
        
        mq_close(mq);
    } else {
        perror("Could not open simulation queue");
    }
}
      Use code with caution.
      Critical Environment Details
      On Linux: 
      • Linking: When compilation occurs via gcc, you must link the POSIX realtime extension library dynamically by appending the -lrt compiler flag:
        bash
        gcc target_app.c -o target_app -lrt
        Use code with caution.
      • Virtual Mount: On modern Linux kernels, you can see and interact with your created message queues inside the system's virtual directory framework via /dev/mqueue/hw_interrupt_q. 
      On VxWorks (RTP): 
      • Component Layer Dependency: Ensure that your kernel bundle profile includes the native POSIX message queue engine option (INCLUDE_POSIX_MQ / mqPxLib). If it is missing from your VIP configuration, mq_open will return an allocation error. 
      • Cross-Boundary Integration: Because POSIX queues exist system-wide within VxWorks, a background module or an ISR executing in Kernel space can execute mq_open and use mq_send to drop interrupt context directly down into a user-space RTP thread effortlessly.

      the interrupt driver is a 3rd party software and have to be file like style for blocking reading. Not sure if POSIX msg Q can mimic it from user space?

      AI Mode reply for the interrupt driver is a 3rd party software and have to be file like style for blocking reading. Not sure if POSIX msg Q can mimic it from user space?

      No, POSIX Message Queues cannot mimic a file-like driver. 
      The 3rd party software uses standard file operations (open, read, close) and expects a file descriptor integer (int fd). POSIX message queues do not produce standard file descriptors; they use a completely different descriptor type (mqd_t), and you interact with them via mq_receive(), not read(). Passing an mqd_t handle or a message queue path to read() will fail immediately with a compilation or runtime error. 
      To keep a file-like layout (open/read) that blocks automatically on both systems from user-space, you need an IPC mechanism that natively produces real file descriptors. 
      The Cross-Platform Strategy: POSIX Pipes
      You can substitute POSIX message queues with Standard POSIX Pipes (pipe()) to simulate the driver. 
      A standard POSIX pipe provides two file descriptors: a read end and a write end. You can pass the read end to your 3rd party software. It behaves exactly like a character device or a driver node—calling read() on it will block the execution thread until data is pushed into the write end. 
      This architecture works out-of-the-box in both Linux user-space and VxWorks RTP user-space without needing root or kernel-level privileges. 
       [ Automated Test Thread ] ---> writes to ---> [ pipe_fds[1] ]
                                                      |
                                                 (Kernel Buffer)
                                                      |
 3rd Party Software Component:                  (Blocks Read)
 [   read(pipe_fds[0], ...)  ] <----------------------+
      Cross-Platform Implementation Example
      1. The Test Harness File Wrapper 
      You can create a small test-fixture initialization file that intercepts the device initialization phase, builds the pipe, and forces the 3rd party code to read from it. 
      c
      #include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdint.h>

// Global array to store the simulation pipe's file descriptors
int sim_hw_pipe[2];

void init_hardware_simulator(void)
{
    // pipe() creates two connected file descriptors: 
    // sim_hw_pipe[0] = Read End (Pass this to your 3rd-party code)
    // sim_hw_pipe[1] = Write End (Use this to inject mock interrupts)
    if (pipe(sim_hw_pipe) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to create cross-platform simulation pipe");
    }
}

// Call this from your background test bench loop to trigger an interrupt event
void inject_mock_interrupt(uint32_t vector)
{
    // Writing to the write-end immediately unblocks the 3rd-party read()
    write(sim_hw_pipe[1], &vector, sizeof(vector));
}
      Use code with caution.
      2. The 3rd-Party App View 
      Your 3rd-party binary accepts the read file descriptor sim_hw_pipe[0] instead of an actual file path string. This allows it to read data blocks sequentially using its internal architecture. 
      c
      void third_party_interrupt_listener(int target_fd)
{
    uint32_t incoming_vector = 0;
    
    printf("3rd Party software started monitoring file descriptor %d...\n", target_fd);
    
    while(1) {
        /*
         * This call BLOCKS natively on Linux and VxWorks RTP.
         * The 3rd party software doesn't know it's a pipe; 
         * it just sees a character file stream.
         */
        ssize_t n = read(target_fd, &incoming_vector, sizeof(incoming_vector));
        
        if (n > 0) {
            printf("[3rd Party Processed Vector]: 0x%08X\n", incoming_vector);
        }
    }
}
      Use code with caution.
      Comparison of Solutions
      Simulation MethodFile-like API (read)?Runs in Linux User Space?Runs in VxWorks RTP?Best Choice For
      POSIX Message Queue❌ No (mq_receive)YesYesCross-platform messaging, but fails file-style requirements.
      pipeDevCreate()Yes (read)❌ NoYesPerfect emulation on VxWorks via string paths, but breaks Linux portability.
      Standard POSIX pipe()Yes (read)YesYesTesting file-based 3rd-party components on both platforms.
      Key Portability Notes
      • Data Stream Consistency: Unlike VxWorks' native message-oriented drivers, a POSIX pipe acts as a continuous byte stream on both systems. If you write two uint32_t items consecutively from the test rig, a larger read statement might pull both variables at once. Ensure your test harness pushes data packets sequentially at the speed your application expects to read them. 
      • VxWorks Compatibility: The POSIX pipe() abstraction runs cleanly inside the VxWorks RTP framework because the underlying file descriptor maps straight into the RTP’s internal I/O table slot. 
      Does the 3rd-party software explicitly require a file path string (e.g., passing "/dev/interrupt0" to an internal open() call), or can you pass a pre-opened file descriptor integer directly into its initialization function?

          Yes, 3rd-party API does require a file path style string and call open().

          AI Mode reply for Yes, 3rd-party API does require a file path style string and call open().

          To successfully compile and test your application on both Linux and VxWorks RTP when the 3rd-party API requires a file path string and calls open(), you can use conditional macros (#ifdef) during compilation. 
          Because Linux and VxWorks have different native APIs for string-addressable blocking file paths, your cross-platform strategy should look like this: 
          • On Linux: Use a POSIX Named Pipe via mkfifo().
          • On VxWorks RTP: Use a Virtual Named Pipe via pipeDevCreate(). 
          The Cross-Platform Mock Architecture
          You can wrap the creation and teardown of the simulated string path inside a small cross-platform simulation library. 
          1. The Simulation Environment Setup (hw_sim.c) 
          This module creates a named blocking string node that the 3rd-party code can call open() and read() against seamlessly. 
          c
          #include <stdio.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

#ifdef __VXWORKS__
#include <pipeDrv.h>  // VxWorks Named Pipe Header
#endif

// A string path that looks like a normal driver node to the 3rd party
#define SIM_HW_PATH "/tmp/mock_interrupt_device"

void create_simulated_hardware_node(void)
{
#ifdef __VXWORKS__
    /* 
     * VxWorks RTP Layer: Creates a blocking virtual device path string.
     * Args: Device name path, max unread messages, message size
     */
    pipeDevCreate(SIM_HW_PATH, 10, sizeof(uint32_t));
#else
    /* 
     * Linux User-space Layer: Creates a standard POSIX FIFO named pipe.
     */
    mkfifo(SIM_HW_PATH, 0666);
#endif
    printf("[SIM] Mock hardware node created at: %s\n", SIM_HW_PATH);
}

void trigger_mock_interrupt(uint32_t vector)
{
    // Both platforms use open() and write() to push data context to the path
    int fd = open(SIM_HW_PATH, O_WRONLY);
    if (fd >= 0) {
        write(fd, &vector, sizeof(vector));
        close(fd);
    } else {
        perror("[SIM] Failed to trigger interrupt");
    }
}

void cleanup_simulated_hardware_node(void)
{
#ifdef __VXWORKS__
    pipeDevDelete(SIM_HW_PATH, TRUE);
#else
    unlink(SIM_HW_PATH);
#endif
}
          Use code with caution.
          2. The 3rd-Party App Environment Simulation 
          When the 3rd-party binary invokes its internal lifecycle, it passes the path string you created, successfully blocking on execution. 
          c
          // Inside your test setup or application initialization
void run_test_cycle(void)
{
    // 1. Create the cross-platform file path abstraction
    create_simulated_hardware_node();

    // 2. Launch your 3rd-party library (represented here conceptually)
    // The 3rd party will do: int fd = open("/tmp/mock_interrupt_device", O_RDONLY);
    // followed by: read(fd, ...) which will naturally block.
    start_third_party_software_thread(SIM_HW_PATH);

    // 3. From your test harness background worker loop, simulate an interrupt
    sleep(2); 
    trigger_mock_interrupt(0xDEADBEEF); // This unblocks the 3rd-party read() instantly
}
          Use code with caution.
          Handling Platform Nuances During Development
          1. Linux Blocking on open(): On Linux, when code calls open(..., O_RDONLY) on a POSIX FIFO (mkfifo), the open() call itself will block until another thread opens the same file for writing (O_WRONLY). To prevent your 3rd-party initialization thread from freezing prematurely on Linux, ensure your test harness background framework initializes or briefly touches the write-end of the pipe immediately after creation. 
          2. VxWorks Path Context: On VxWorks, paths can use any structure, but creating them inside a /tmp/ or device-like syntax allows you to maintain exact configuration symmetry with your Linux setup. 
          3. Automating Builds: You can use your build compiler to automatically differentiate target environments without manually editing source files.
            • On Linux: Built via standard GCC (gcc hw_sim.c -o test_bin)
            • On VxWorks: Built with the Wind River compiler (ccpentium, ccarm, etc.), which automatically defines the __VXWORKS__ macro flags. 
          Are you using a Makefile or a CMake build setup to compile this across both target environments? I can help configure the platform flags appropriately if needed.

          AI Mode reply for I am using CMake

          To seamlessly compile this setup across platforms, you can leverage CMake to detect whether you are compiling for a local Linux desktop or cross-compiling for a VxWorks RTP. 
          When you pass the official Wind River toolchain file to CMake (-DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=...), it implicitly sets a platform variable called VXWORKS to TRUE. You can trap this logic inside your build file to inject the platform-specific flags. 
          The Cross-Platform CMakeLists.txt
          This template handles your mock file abstractions and automatically assigns the native compile definitions and dependencies depending on the target ecosystem. 
          cmake
          cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.12)
project(HardwareSimulationFixture C)

# Ensure standard C99/C11 features are accessible
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 99)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

# Define your project executable target
add_executable(hw_test_app 
    main.c 
    hw_sim.c
)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Platform-Specific Adjustments
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
if(VXWORKS)
    message(STATUS "Configuring build layout for Wind River VxWorks...")
    
    # 1. Inform your source files that they are executing under VxWorks
    target_compile_definitions(hw_test_app PRIVATE TARGET_OS_VXWORKS)
    
    # 2. Add VxWorks runtime linkages if your RTP build requires strict symbol maps
    # target_link_libraries(hw_test_app PRIVATE ...)

else()
    message(STATUS "Configuring build layout for Linux Desktop Host...")
    
    # 1. Inform your source files that they are executing under Linux
    target_compile_definitions(hw_test_app PRIVATE TARGET_OS_LINUX)
    
    # 2. Linux requires linking POSIX realtime system libraries for blocking abstractions
    target_link_libraries(hw_test_app PRIVATE rt)
endif()

          Personalizing

          AI Mode reply for Yes, please show me the CTest

          To orchestrate this cross-platform hardware simulation as a standardized test, you can integrate CTest directly into your CMakeLists.txt. 
          Since testing a blocking read requires two concurrent actions (the 3rd-party code waiting on the file path, and a test harness writing an interrupt vector to unblock it), you need a way to run them asynchronously. 
          The most robust, cross-platform way to test this without dealing with complex multithreading code inside your test environment is to split the architecture into two separate, lightweight executables: 
          1. test_listener: Simulates the 3rd-party software component (open() and block read()).
          2. test_injector: Simulates the hardware ISR (open() and write() an interrupt vector). 
          Step 1: Update your CMakeLists.txt for CTest
          Add CTest support to your build script, compiling the listener and the injector as standalone targets. 
          cmake
          cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.12)
project(HardwareSimulationFixture C)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 99)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

# Enable the CTest testing framework infrastructure
enable_testing()

# 1. The Listener Target (Simulates your 3rd-party blocking software)
add_executable(test_listener listener_app.c hw_sim_common.c)

# 2. The Injector Target (Simulates the test suite firing the HW interrupt)
add_executable(test_injector injector_app.c hw_sim_common.c)

# Set platform macros
if(VXWORKS)
    target_compile_definitions(test_listener PRIVATE TARGET_OS_VXWORKS)
    target_compile_definitions(test_injector PRIVATE TARGET_OS_VXWORKS)
else()
    target_compile_definitions(test_listener PRIVATE TARGET_OS_LINUX)
    target_compile_definitions(test_injector PRIVATE TARGET_OS_LINUX)
    target_link_libraries(test_listener PRIVATE rt)
    target_link_libraries(test_injector PRIVATE rt)
endif()

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Define CTest Test Cases
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Test Case A: Verify the Node can initialize and clean up properly
add_test(NAME Test_HW_Node_Lifecycle COMMAND test_injector --setup-only)

# Test Case B: The integration test loop
# CTest executes the listener app, which expects a mock interrupt 
# vector (e.g., 0xDEADBEEF) within a 5-second timeout window.
add_test(NAME Test_Interrupt_Blocking_Read COMMAND test_listener)
set_tests_properties(Test_Interrupt_Blocking_Read PROPERTIES TIMEOUT 5)
          Use code with caution.
          Step 2: The Independent Target Source Files
          hw_sim_common.c & hw_sim_common.h 
          This holds the shared platform logic we built earlier: 
          c
          #include <stdio.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

#ifdef TARGET_OS_VXWORKS
  #include <pipeDrv.h>
#endif

#define SIM_HW_PATH "/tmp/mock_interrupt_device"

void create_node(void) {
#ifdef TARGET_OS_VXWORKS
    pipeDevCreate(SIM_HW_PATH, 10, sizeof(unsigned int));
#else
    mkfifo(SIM_HW_PATH, 0666);
#endif
}

void destroy_node(void) {
#ifdef TARGET_OS_VXWORKS
    pipeDevDelete(SIM_HW_PATH, 1);
#else
    unlink(SIM_HW_PATH);
#endif
}
          Use code with caution.
          listener_app.c (The 3rd-Party Mimic) 
          This app boots, sets up the virtual environment, blocks until the injector feeds it, and evaluates success. 
          c
          #include <stdio.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include "hw_sim_common.h"

int main(void) {
    // 1. Ensure a clean node exists for the test run
    destroy_node(); 
    create_node();

    printf("[Listener] Opening %s (blocking mode)...\n", SIM_HW_PATH);
    int fd = open(SIM_HW_PATH, O_RDONLY);
    if (fd < 0) return 1; // Test Failed

    unsigned int interrupt_vector = 0;
    printf("[Listener] Blocking on read()...\n");
    
    // Natively blocks here across both Linux and VxWorks
    int bytes_read = read(fd, &interrupt_vector, sizeof(interrupt_vector));
    close(fd);

    if (bytes_read == sizeof(interrupt_vector) && interrupt_vector == 0xDEADBEEF) {
        printf("[SUCCESS] Received expected vector: 0x%08X\n", interrupt_vector);
        destroy_node();
        return 0; // Test Passed!
    }

    printf("[FAILURE] Unexpected data size or vector value.\n");
    destroy_node();
    return 1; // Test Failed
}

          injector_app.c (The Test Suite Executioner) 
          This program is invoked externally or via a script to fire the vector. 
          c
          #include <stdio.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include "hw_sim_common.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    if (argc > 1 && strcmp(argv[1], "--setup-only") == 0) {
        create_node();
        destroy_node();
        return 0;
    }

    // Fire the interrupt vector down the pipe line
    int fd = open(SIM_HW_PATH, O_WRONLY);
    if (fd < 0) return 1;

    unsigned int test_vector = 0xDEADBEEF;
    write(fd, &test_vector, sizeof(test_vector));
    close(fd);
    
    printf("[Injector] Fired interrupt vector 0xDEADBEEF\n");
    return 0;
}

          Step 3: Executing the Automated CTest Suite
          Running on Linux (Desktop Integration) 
          On your development station, compile and run CTest. You will kick off the test_listener and fire the test_injector sequentially or asynchronously: 
          bash
          mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
make

# 1. Run the listener test target in the background
ctest -R Test_Interrupt_Blocking_Read &

# 2. Fire the interrupt helper to unblock CTest and verify execution success
sleep 0.5
./test_injector

          Running on VxWorks (Target Deployment) 
          Inside your VxWorks environment, your CI/CD test system runs the generated binaries inside the RTP shell instance: 
          vxworks
          /* Run the listener inside its own RTP thread task */
rtpSp "test_listener.vxe"

/* Invoke the injector to fulfill the interrupt dependency path */
rtpSp "test_injector.vxe"
          Use code with caution.
          Because test_listener exits with 0 upon identifying 0xDEADBEEF, CTest registers the cycle as a complete match validation profile.
